sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The power systems are quite complex structures that include
systems such as generators, loads, and transmission lines.
Over the years, energy demand has increased due to the
loads added to the system. This energy demand reveals the
necessity of including new production units and transmission
lines in the system. The Transmission Network Expansion
Planning (TNEP) problem is concerned with ensuring the
integration of new generation units into the system in order
to meet energy demand and identifying the optimal location
The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and

for new transmission lines, with the objective of minimizing
cost [1], [2]. The TNEP problem was initially addressed by
Garver in 1970 [3]. In his study, Garver incorporated a sixth
bus, comprising a 545 MW production unit, into the five-
bus system, which had a consumption of 760 MW and a
production of 215 MW. His objective was to identify the opti-
mal location for the transmission lines in order to facilitate
the most cost-effective distribution of power throughout the
system. In his study, Garver employed a model that considers
the active power balance of the bus in question. Subsequently,
this methodology was further developed, resulting in the
emergence of the DC load flow method. In this method,
the resistances of the lines and the reactive power flow are

not considered. Accordingly, only the active power flow is
considered.
Rider et al., introduced the AC power flow method to the
literature in 2007 in order to evaluate the neglected param-
eters in the DC load flow and to provide a more realistic
solution [4]. As mentioned, although AC power flow evalu-
ates the neglected parameters, it makes the complex TNEP
problem even more complicated. For this reason, the DC
power flow method has remained an option for researchers.
Although solutions are made with the AC power flow method
today [5], [6], the DC power flow method is also used because
it produces fast solutions and gives results with acceptable
accuracy [1], [7], [8], [9].
The TNEP problem planning can be examined in two parts.
Determining the location and number of lines according to a
single planning stage is called Static TNEP (STNEP). The
realization of planning for certain time intervals is called
Dynamic TNEP (DTNEP). The DTNEP problem was first
solved by Dodu and Merlin in 1981 [10]. In DTNEP studies,
solutions can be made by taking into account various features
such as inflation rates, environmental changes, equipment
wear, and annual load increases. Researchers have tried to
develop an effective method to solve the TNEP , which has
a multidimensional complex engineering problem. In 1970,
the TNEP problem was first solved by Garver. Mathematical
optimization methods have been used to solve the prob-
lem [3]. Linear Programming (LP) [3], Mixed Integer Linear
Programming (MILP) [11], [12], Mixed Integer Nonlin-
ear Programming (MINLP) [13], and Mixed Binary Linear
Programming (MBLP) [14] can be given as examples of
mathematical optimization methods used. Because the TNEP
problem is a high-dimensional complex problem, solutions
made with mathematical methods require high computational
times. This makes the solution of the problem quite difficult.
To overcome the limitations caused by mathematical meth-
ods, researchers have turned to heuristic methods. Heuristic
methods provide sufficient solution quality at certain times as
well as low computational time. Some of the heuristic opti-
mization methods used in the TNEP problem are the Fuzzy
Fault Tree Method [15], Heuristic Algorithm with Fuzzy
Logic [16], and Sensitivity Analysis [17]. Later, researchers
turned to meta-heuristic optimization algorithms because of
both their low computational time compared to mathematical
methods and their ability to get very close to the solution.
Meta-heuristic optimization algorithms use heuristic opti-
mization algorithms iteratively. For this reason, although they
have more computational load than heuristic methods, they
have a lower computational load than mathematical methods.
In addition to the acceptable increase in computational load,
it provides solutions with high accuracy. Considering those
new constraints such as security, environmental issues, and
maintenance and repair costs can be added to TNEP studies
that include investment costs, the complexity of the prob-
lem highlights the advantages of meta-heuristic optimization
methods even more.
In 1996 and 1997, STNEP research, encompassing invest-
ment costs and Loss of Load costs (LOL), were executed
utilizing the Simulated Annealing (SA) technique, along-
side the development of a parallel SA algorithm [18], [19].
A Genetic Algorithm (GA) was introduced in 2000 to address
the issue [20]. In 2001, the Tabu Search (TS) methodology
was employed to reduce investment costs. The findings indi-
cated that it is an effective method for addressing the STNEP
problem [21]. In 2002, the STNEP problem, which seeks to
reduce investment costs and line losses, was addressed with a
hybrid approach utilizing Artificial Neural Networks (ANN),
Genetic Algorithms (GA), and Tabu Search (TS) algorithms,
demonstrating the efficacy of the suggested method [22].
In 2004, the Enhanced Genetic Algorithm (EGA) was favored
for addressing the Deterministic Time-Dependent Network
Equilibrium Problem (DTNEP) [23]. In 2010, the Discrete
Particle Swarm Optimization (DPSO) technique was devel-
oped to optimize transmission line loading [24]. In 2014, the
STNEP issue was addressed via an enhanced PSO algorithm
(LPSO) [25]. In 2017, the Multi Group PSO algorithm
(MGPSO) was introduced to address the unique STNEP
problem [26]. In 2019, a DTNEP study utilized the Ant
Colony Optimization (ACO) algorithm to assess operating
and investment expenditures. A comparative evaluation of
MILP and ACO algorithms revealed that the ACO algorithm
demonstrated enhanced performance regarding computing
time and solution quality [27]. In 2020, a Static and Dynamic
TNEP analysis was conducted employing an Adaptive Salp
Swarm Optimization Algorithm (ASSO) [28]. The STNEP
investigation was conducted in 2021 with the Discrete Arti-
ficial Bee Colony Algorithm (DABC) [29]. In that year, the
DTNEP study was conducted with the LSHADE-SPACMA
algorithm, which also considers the N-1 reliability con-
straint [30]. In 2022, the STNEP and DTNEP investigation
was conducted with the Improved Binary Bat Algorithm
(IBBA) [31]. The STNEP study was conducted in 2023 uti-
lizing a novel hybrid GA-PSO algorithm. A related study
demonstrated that the GA-PSO algorithm outperformed both
GA and PSO algorithms in minimizing investment costs [2].
These works demonstrate the significance of employing
meta-heuristic optimization strategies to address the TNEP
problem.
On the basis of the literature review, TNEP is pertinent
to the identification of the expansion policy of the transmis-
sion grid to serve future electricity demand efficiently and
economically while at the same time taking into account the
operational limitations, legal requirement for the environ-
ment, cost of investment and system reliability. This problem
has a large-scale mixed integer and nonlinear form and signif-
icant technical, economic, and environmental constraints. For
this reason alone, traditional mathematical optimization tech-
niques cannot solve the problem effectively because they rely
on slope information and can be trapped in the local optimum.
That is, while linear programming and even mixed-integer
programming can be employed for traditional mathematical

is founded on the supposition that the opposite of a candidate
solution is closer to the global optimum than the candidate
solution itself, providing a better overall review of the search
space of the optimal solution. Here, by comparing the current
solution with its opposite solution, OBL enhances the chances
of finding a better area and thereby avoids trapping in the
local optima, which in turn optimizes the solution search
process very efficiently. Moreover, OBL is always effective
in avoiding solution stagnation by preserving the population
differentiation and making the algorithm additional adaptive
to solve high- and complex problems. That is a valuable
application of the double assessment framework because it
enforces a switch between exploitation and exploration that
can improve the metaheuristic algorithms and the optimiza-
tion. Thus, over time, various OBL approaches have been
documented in the literature. Examples of these methodolo-
gies include Classical OBL [43], Quasi OBL [44], Quasi
Reflection OBL [45], Super OBL [46], Elite OBL [47],
Random OBL [48], Dynamic OBL [49], and Probabilistic
OBL [50].
This study aims to establish candidate selection strategies
for solutions by using the FDB selection method to the
Coati Optimization Algorithm [32]. The FDB approach was
employed to assist the COA algorithm in avoiding local solu-
tion traps and achieving convergence to the global solution
point. Multiple iterations were generated by implementing
the FDB method at distinct position update points within
the algorithm, and various comparisons were conducted to
identify the optimal version among them. The comparison
results indicate that the COA algorithm using the optimal
FDB version is designated as FDBCOA. Following the iden-
tification of the optimal FDB variation tailored to several
application domains for the COA algorithm, OBL techniques
were employed in the initial population to enhance solu-
tion diversity and augment the search capability for the
optimal solution This study employs eight distinct OBL
approaches from the literature to identify the most efficient
method and to provide a framework for future research. The
optimal OBL technique was identified based on the out-
comes of the simulated simulations. The FDBCOA algorithm
using OBL methodologies is designated FDBCOA-OBL. The
FDBCOA-OBL algorithm has been implemented to address
the TNEP problem, and its efficacy in resolving the engi-
neering issue is examined. The investment expenditures for
Garver’s 6-bus test system, the IEEE 25-bus test system,
and the Colombian 93-bus test system are assessed using the
FDBCOA-OBL algorithm.
The key contributions of the paper are delineated as
follows:
• This study introduces the application of FDB and OBL
approaches to enhance the efficacy of the COA algorithm,
as reported in 2023, in identifying optimal solutions for opti-
mization problems. The efficacy of the suggested approach in
identifying the optimal solution was evidenced by a simula-
tion study utilizing CEC2020 and CEC 2022 benchmark test
functions [51], [52]. The efficacy of the suggested algorithm
was evaluated across various problem dimensions and popu-
lation sizes.
• Three distinct FDB selection methodologies were
employed in the COA algorithm. This paper introduces the
COA algorithm, exhibiting the optimal FDB variation, to the
literature for the first time as FDBCOA.
• In the initial population creation phase, eight distinct
OBL methods were employed to enhance the solution diver-
sity within the solution space of the FDBCOA algorithm. The
results of the simulation studies allowed for the identification
of the FDBCOA algorithm with the most effective OBL
variation. Simulation studies present the success of the COA
algorithm, where OBL and FDB selection methods are used
as a hybrid, in solving benchmark test functions for the first
time in the literature and create a different perspective for
researchers.
• The success of the FDBCOA-OBL algorithm in solving
different types of optimization problems has been substanti-
ated through a statistical evaluation of simulation outcomes
using the Wilcoxon and Friedman tests.
• The suggested method was employed to address the
TNEP problem, a contemporary challenge in electric power
system planning, and its efficacy in resolving practical
engineering issues was examined. The algorithm’s efficacy
in addressing the TNEP problem was examined across
low, medium, and high-scale test systems. This work
examined the efficacy of an optimization algorithm, con-
structed using FDB and OBL approaches, in addressing the
TNEP problem, introducing it to the literature for the first
time.
• The results obtained demonstrate the effectiveness of the
FDBCOA-OBL algorithm in achieving the optimal solution.
This paper aims to present a novel and robust optimization
technique, termed FDBCOA-OBL, to the literature.
This study consists of 4 sections after the introduction. The
other sections are presented below in order:
• The mathematical model of the Static and Dynamic
TNEP problem is presented in Section II.
• The proposed FDBCOA-OBL algorithm is introduced in
Section III. The subsections analyze the settings used in the
experimental study, benchmark packages, and the results of
all experimental studies.
• The solution of TNEP problems with the proposed
algorithm is presented in Section IV. Test systems and solu-
tions are analyzed in the subsections.
• The results of the study, discussions, and future work are
summarized in Section V.

sections.title: MATHEMATICAL MODEL OF STATIC AND DYNAMIC
sections.text:
TNEP PROBLEM
The growth in energy consumption over time has created a
pressing need to integrate new generation facilities and trans-
mission infrastructure into existing power systems [1], [2].
In particular, the investment expenses recorded as expenses
related to the criteria for different test systems include the
financial costs of establishing new transmission structures or
VOLUME 13, 2025 35071
M. Demirbas et al.: Enhanced Coati Optimization Algorithm for Static and Dynamic TNEP Problems
strengthening old ones in the execution of the TNEP . These
costs include dollar figures associated with some features
of transmission lines like the size, the voltage level, type of
conductor, and cost of construction often including the cost
of employing people, materials and tools. The computation
also takes into account other costs that are not variable in
nature, which include land procurement costs and permission
charges, as well as costs that make up operational costs,
including costs of maintenance of the structures all through
until the lifetime of the infrastructure is depleted. For the test
systems, general cost coefficients are employed for the sys-
tematic assessment of the different optimization techniques
and they may not be very significantly different from the
actual cost volatility. In practice, these investment expenses
are simplified in test systems for further benchmarking of
different algorithms. For instance, a fixed cost for every kilo-
meter of the transmission line might be postulated and other
operational or geographical features like terrain or develop-
ment are often omitted due to simplicity. However, in reality,
the fixed investment costs can be much higher due to factors
like zoning and land availability constraints, harsh environ-
mental conditions and policy change, and other problems
related to project location. This can affect the methodology
of easily applied methods primarily designed and used in test
systems.
To compare these costs with actual system expansion costs,
one would need to adjust the results of the test systems
by externally scaling them by using real numbers, includ-
ing inflation rates, regional differences in cost and other
constraints which are not incorporated into test systems.
A detailed comparison can then best demonstrate the useful-
ness of the proposed method because it can reveal, from the
test systems, the practical performance and cost effectiveness
of the solutions it proposes in real life situations. Such an
analysis makes the method more realistic and ensures that
anyone intends to apply the method when solving large scale
dispersed power networks has the confidence of not only
the theoretical but the actual application of the method [53],
[54], [55].
Said more plainly, the TNEP problem aims to provide
a means for ensuring the introduction of new generation
units into the system and, determining the location where
additional transmission lines are most effectively sited while
ensuring the most cost-effective solution. Regarding the
objective of the fitness function developed for the TNEP
problem, it intends to verify if the constraints are also
being violated in the process of obtaining the optimal
solution of the problem. The TNEP problem includes a
number of fundamentals; load flow balance between the
buses, load flow limit of the transmission line, generation
limit and line restriction addition capability. To assess these
constraints, it is required to calculate the load flow data
between the buses. To this end, the required DC load flow
data of the power systems was obtained with the help of
MA TPOWER[56].
A. DESCRIPTION OF STATIC TNEP PROBLEM
The fitness function used in the Static TNEP problem
includes the penalty function and the objective function that
checks whether the constraints are violated. While the load
balance on the buses constitutes the equality constraint; the
load flow limits, the limits of the production units and the
number of lines that can be added between the buses con-
stitute the inequality constraints. While adding lines to the
system, the constraints must also be checked and the specified
limits must not be exceeded. The objective function of the
problem includes the investment cost. Each line to be added
between the busess has an investment cost. The investment
cost will also increase as the number of lines to be added
increases. In systems that grow depending on the increase in
demand power over the years, it is aimed to add lines between
the buses at the lowest cost.
The fitness and the objective functions used to solve the
Static TNEP problem are given in Equations (1) and (2),
respectively [57], [58].

B. DESCRIPTION OF DYNAMIC TNEP PROBLEM
The dynamic multistage TNEP methodology used in this
work to analyze the 93-bus system enables a systematic
means of incrementally and adaptively planning transmis-
sion network expansion across stages of time. But first, the
existing network has to be evaluated for immediate problems
and growth opportunities in order to set a starting reference
point for further development. Of especial importance is the
forecasting of load growth and of renewable energy gener-
ating capacities to be added at each stage of the planning
horizon. These forecasts incorporate risks, which include
demand change, varying level of renewable generation and
changes in policies. In each phase, an optimization model is
formulated and solved to find an economical solution that
will satisfy the reliability requirements, other performance
parameters, and legal provisions. It puts into consideration
the overruling effect from one stage to another in planning so
as to have a health proper planning in the overall planning
period. The method also addresses uncertainties systemat-
ically by using probabilistic and scenarios approaches by
emulating the variability in load and generation to arrive at
solution. This approach helps to select investments that are
good in the number of scenarios of the future state and pro-
vides system dependability and flexibility. Another flexibility
is an iterative feedback loop by which the plan is updated
as and when actual outcomes differ from expected values.
Through solving the specified problem on the 93-bus system
this method shows its ability to phase investments, minimize
costs, and integrate new developments of energy systems
making it a practical and viable approach to large-scale power
system planning [59], [60], [61].

Dynamic TNEP problem are shown in Equations (8) and (9),

Dehghani et al., in 2023. It was created by taking inspira-
tion from the strategies that Coatimundis, mammals native
to the southwestern United States, South America, Cen-
tral America, and Mexico, follow when attacking Iguanas
and their behaviors when escaping from predators [32].
This algorithm initially creates a random population using

they are then attacked by the coatis. This technique allows
COA to traverse multiple regions within the search space
and execute the exploration phase. In the design of COA, the
optimal member of the population is regarded as the position
of the iguana. As stated in Equation (17) [32], the positional

1) IDENTIFYING THE BEST FDBCOA ALGORITHM IN
CEC 2020 AND CEC 2022 BENCHMARK TEST FUNCTIONS
An experimental investigation was undertaken to evaluate the
efficacy of the created FDBCOA algorithms in the search
process. The goal of the experimental investigation is to
elucidate the impact of the versions developed with FDB
and to identify the optimal version. The performances of the
COA, FDBCOA1, FDBCOA2, and FDBCOA3 algorithms
were assessed using the CEC2020 and CEC2022 benchmark
packages. The modifications implemented to guarantee the
reliability and objectivity of the experimental investigation
are outlined below.
• The greatest number of fitness function evaluations
(maxFEs) serves as the termination condition. In both
the CEC2020 and CEC2022 benchmark suites, the
maxFEs are established at 10000 ∗Dim. ‘‘Dim’’ is
defined as the magnitude of the problem.
• The CEC2020 benchmark suite analyzed dimensions
of 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, and 100, whereas the CEC2022
benchmark suite focused on 10 and 20 dimensions
to assess the algorithms’ convergence performance
towards the ideal solution.
• The efficacy of the COA and FDBCOA algorithms was
evaluated over varying population sizes of 30, 50, and
100.
• The algorithms for the CEC2020 and CEC2022
benchmarking packages were executed 51 times.
To enhance the significance of the data, Fried-
man and Wilcoxon statistical analysis methods were
employed. Consequently, the success levels of the
algorithms were determined, and comparisons were
conducted.

The Wilcoxon and Friedman techniques were employed
for the statistical assessment of the COA, FDBCOA1, FDB-
COA2, and FDBCOA3 algorithms. The Friedman method
results facilitated the identification of the most effective
algorithm for addressing the CEC2020 and CEC2022 bench-
mark packages. The Friedman scores of the algorithms across
various parameters are presented in Table 2 for CEC2020 and
in Table 3 for CEC2022.
The average Friedman scores for the algorithms are dis-
played in Table 4, derived from the data in Tables 2 and 3.
Based on the average Friedman scores, FDBCOA1 is iden-
tified as the most effective algorithm among the evaluated
algorithms. The fundamental COA algorithm is the least
effective among the algorithms.

drew 110 problems, and won 166 problems. The FDBCOA1
algorithm demonstrated excellent performance, achieving a
win rate of 58.86%, a draw rate of 39.01%, and a loss rate of
2.13%.
Moreover, Wilcoxon pairwise test results proved that
algorithm FDBCOA1 consistently outperformed the base-
line algorithm COA in CEC2020 and CEC2022 benchmarks,
especially at higher dimensions and larger population sizes.
FDBCOA1 showed dominant performance with high win
rates and minimal or no losses, but occasional poor perfor-
mance was observed at lower dimensions and more complex
problem instances, especially at P = 100. Algorithm FDB-
COA2, more specifically, showed moderate and consistently
improved results, and it had better result than COA, par-
ticularly at medium and higher order dimensions. However,
FDBCOA2 did not match the performance of FDBCOA1,
with occasional ties and less sure shot wins. On the other
hand, the performance of the algorithm FDBCOA3 for both
benchmarks were significantly lower than that of COA; it
often reached only ties or occasionally slightly outperformed
COA. It faced severe scalability problems, especially on
more complex problems. Overall, the Wilcoxon test con-
firmed that FDBCOA1 was the most robust algorithm against
COA, followed by FDBCOA2, which gradually improved,
and FDBCOA3 remained the least effective.
The No Free Lunch (NFL) [62] Theorem states that there
is no optimization algorithm that can outperform all others
on an average to all the problems. Cues well adapted to
algorithms for specific problems are generally worse than
those that have quite different architectures at heart. However,
differences in how the exploration and exploitation processes
occurred, how sensitive these algorithms were to the param-
eters given, or how the intrinsic bias of the algorithm designs
might have led to these algorithms converging early or even
inefficiently on certain problem types. The stochastic prop-
erties of these algorithms also produce random performance
and, in some instances, poor performance as well. Accord-
ing to the NFL theorem, these factors imply that a search
algorithm such as FDBCOA1, FDBCOA2, or FDBCOA3 will
always be comparatively slower to COA on some problems.
✓ Convergence analysis of FDBCOA algorithm variations
This section presents assessments of the convergence
capabilities of the developed FDBCOA versions through
convergence and box-plot curves. The CEC 2020 and
CEC 2022 benchmark packages encompass problem types
from four distinct function categories: ‘‘unimodal,’’ ‘‘basic,’’
‘‘hybrid,’’ and ‘‘composition.’’ Figure 2 shows the conver-
gence curves and boxplot graphs illustrating the solutions of

2020 benchmark package, with a population size of 50.
Upon analyzing the convergence curves, it is evident

for the CEC 2020 benchmark suite outperform the stan-
dard COA algorithm in reducing the function error value.
Among the proposed FDB versions, the FDBCOA1 algorithm
demonstrates superior efficacy compared to FDBCOA2 and
FDBCOA3. This validates the assessment conducted by
Friedman and Wilcoxon analyses. Box-plot illustrations

evaluate the performance of optimization algorithms to solve
problems efficiently when the complexity increases due to
increasing problem sizes in optimization problems.
This method evaluates the algorithms’ practical and
robust behavior to solve complex, large-scale, and evolv-
ing real-world problems and their robustness in maintaining
solution quality by providing critical insights into computa-
tional efficiency, runtime behavior, resource usage, memory

anticipated that in the course of the optimization process,
the algorithms would adequately adapt to the increasing
sizes of the target problem without performance deteri-
oration, and thereby enable convergence to the desired
optimum solution. By means of scalability evaluation, the
algorithms can be tested for their effectiveness for solving
real-world optimization problems that have real-world appeal
and require dependable solutions.

The OBL strategy evaluates the present solution candidates’
positions identified by the algorithms against the fitness
values of their opponents’ positions. The comparison yields
the optimal fitness value, and the solution candidate asso-
ciated with this value is chosen. The preceding section
demonstrated that FDBCOA1 is the superior variant of the
COA algorithm developed using the FDB selection approach.
This section focuses on generating the initial population of
the FDBCOA1 algorithm via the OBL technique. The objec-
tive is to identify the best effective option by employing
eight distinct OBL methodologies. The mathematical formu-
lations of the OBL strategies employed are presented in this
subsection.
